source: Figueiredo (2025) Designing Smarter Conversational Agents for Kids: Lessons from Cognitive Work and Means-Ends Analyses
finding: Rare case where a full Cognitive Work Analysis (CWA) was used to derive a prompt scaffold for an LLM. Study 1 mapped child-agent work; Study 2 tested the derived recipe prompt on GPT-4o-mini.
numbers: Study 1: 23 participants (9 Brazilian children aged 9-11 with parents, plus teachers), 7 weeks, about 23 h video; 3 agent functions found (School, Discovery, Entertainment). Study 2: 1,200 simulated exchanges. Recipe vs plain prompt: similarity to grade level Welch t(2980)=6.16, Cohen d=0.225 [0.150,0.300]; coherence partial eta2=0.012; question depth rank-biserial r=0.167.
limits: Simulated children, not real ones. Question depth and diversity were counted from question words, so validity is weak. Effect sizes are small. No ablation against a non-CWA expert prompt, so the CWA step itself is not isolated. Single author, preprint.
agent_relevance: Shows the pipeline CWA to prompt scaffold is feasible, but the gain over a plain prompt is small and the CWA contribution is untested. Do not claim WDA improves LLM output from this.

source: Figueiredo (2025) recipe prompt question-count result
finding: Plain GPT-4o-mini almost never asked scaffolding questions; the recipe prompt asked many.
numbers: Poisson model of question count: incidence rate ratio 0.004 for plain vs recipe (z=-22.71, p<.001); diversity IRR 0.26 (z=-38.38). Temperature had no effect (F(1,2996)=0.27, p=.61).
limits: The huge ratio mostly shows that a prompt that says to ask questions makes the model ask questions. It is a manipulation check as much as a result.
agent_relevance: Cheap evidence that a role and goal structure in the prompt changes behaviour; says little about whether the work-analysis content was the active ingredient.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) STRATA: Self-Maintaining Structured Experience Graphs for Self-Evolving Language Agents
finding: Agent memory built as a typed three-layer abstraction hierarchy (skills and code, task workflows, meta workflows). Not Rasmussen's hierarchy, but the same idea: store knowledge at different levels of abstraction and link them.
numbers: Four benchmarks (AppWorld, WebArena, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld), 2 frozen backbones, 7 baselines. AppWorld Test-Challenge SGC 46.5+-2.3 vs A-Mem 42.2+-2.6; WebArena 45.6+-1.6 vs 41.0+-2.2 (MemEvolve); ALFWorld 98.6+-0.9 vs 96.3+-1.9 (MemGen). 812 WebArena tasks condensed to 112 workflows under 16 meta nodes.
limits: Not separable from the best baseline on AppWorld Test-Normal or ScienceWorld (23 tasks, SD 3.6-15.0); authors decline to claim a ScienceWorld win. Preprint (Oct 2026). Layer names are the authors' own, not from work analysis.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping a typed, levelled store (principle, procedure, step) instead of one flat pool. Gains are modest and uneven.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) STRATA negative transfer result
finding: Flat memory of concrete procedures can make an agent worse than no memory. A contrast edge between directionally opposite goals repairs it.
numbers: Hermes memory scores 30.4/35.8 TGC on AppWorld Test-Normal vs memoryless 62.8/66.9; ScienceWorld 48.3/55.8 vs 75.7/80.6; find-living task -100 (Flash) and -80 (Pro). Contrast edges lift ScienceWorld 78.7 to 89.8 (hand-placed) to 96.7 (rule-based); ALFWorld 89.5 to 98.6.
limits: Ablation on same seeds; the rule is built on an operator lexicon, which is domain specific. End-to-end success also depends on the backbone honouring the warning.
agent_relevance: Relevant to S0: a problem-class gate must separate goals that look alike but have opposite direction or purpose. Surface similarity is the failure mode.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) STRATA memory growth and cost
finding: Unbounded memory hurts; a bounded, abstracting memory is cheaper and better.
numbers: With forgetting off the workflow store grows to 269 nodes injecting 48.7 lines per task and scores lower than a bounded 201-node memory. Cost on DeepSeek-V4-Pro: STRATA 58.7 s, 11.7 steps, 23.3 memory lines per task vs MemGen 72.4 s, 19.4 lines; authors claim 44% fewer injected lines than the most context-hungry baseline.
limits: Authors say they report two consistent observations, not a controlled scaling experiment.
agent_relevance: Abstraction layers control context load. Fits our rule against flooding the prompt.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) STRATA component ablation
finding: Removing any single mechanism costs accuracy; the tag term and contrast edges matter most.
numbers: Ablation on DeepSeek-V4-Pro; for example the no-pressure-GC row reads 70.6 / 50.8 (AppWorld TGC/SGC) / 41.0 / 96.6 / 94.4 / 70.7 across environments.
limits: Numbers read from a table row in text extraction; columns follow the paper's table order.
agent_relevance: Layered store plus maintenance, not layering alone, is what holds up.

source: Chang et al. (2025) ASHiTA: Automatic Scene-grounded Hierarchical Task Analysis
finding: LLM does hierarchical task analysis (HTA, a close cousin of work analysis): it breaks a high-level task into subtasks, alternating with building a 3D scene graph so the breakdown depends on what is in the environment.
numbers: Sequential setting, 205 tasks from SG3D over 8 HM3DSem scenes, GPT-4o-mini. Subtask recall / precision / task accuracy: ASHiTA 10.39 / 20.6 / 9.27 vs Hydra+GPT 9.43 / 15.51 / 4.88 and HOV-SG+GPT 4.55 / 4.87 / 1.95. Ablation without hierarchy refinement t-acc 6.83, without top-down pruning 5.37.
limits: Absolute scores are low (task accuracy under 10 percent in the realistic setting). With ground-truth labels, GPT alone reached 36.1 t-acc (Hydra GT Seg), above ASHiTA's non-GT result. Robotics setting, not human work.
agent_relevance: Task breakdown is environment-dependent, which is the point of domain analysis; letting the LLM break tasks down without the domain gives redundant, tangential subtasks (low precision).

source: Chang et al. (2025) ASHiTA ground-truth setting
finding: With ideal visual-language alignment ASHiTA beats fine-tuned grounding baselines but still trails GPT given ground-truth labels.
numbers: Table 3: ASHiTA (GT Pos) 15.12 / 34.47 / 16.59 and (GT Pos + Txt Emb) 17.06 / 18.98 / 14.63 vs Hydra (GT Seg)+GPT 38.71 / 34.39 / 36.1 (recall / precision / task accuracy).
limits: Gap is blamed on missing relations such as next-to in the scene graph.
agent_relevance: Domain structure helps only if the representation keeps the relations that matter.

source: Simkute et al. (2024) Ironies of Generative AI: Understanding and mitigating productivity loss in human-AI interactions
finding: Review that names ecological interface design (EID, built on the abstraction hierarchy) as one of five fixes for GenAI productivity loss. Four causes: shift from producing to evaluating, workflow restructuring, interruptions, easy tasks made easier and hard tasks harder.
numbers: No new experiment. Cites EID results for reduced workload and better performance in aviation risk management, medical settings, and assisted driving. Cites that Copilot users failed to complete tasks more often than with plain autocomplete (study [118]).
quote: EID emphasizes designing interfaces that reflect users' perceptual constraints within a work environment
limits: Argument paper. EID evidence is from older non-LLM domains. No test of EID applied to a GenAI tool.
agent_relevance: The only mainstream LLM-HCI paper found that calls for work-domain-based design. Ties to S0: know the job's real task sequence before the model offers help.

source: Simkute et al. (2024) EID recommendations for GenAI
finding: Concrete EID advice: show several abstraction levels at once (high-level pseudo-code to low-level code), map suggestions to what they affect beyond the insertion point, and respect the natural task sequence (plan before code).
numbers: Qualitative. Example: expert dermatologists were confused when explanations ignored domain context (skin texture); explainability worked best when combined with insights from medical experts.
limits: Design guidance, not tested.
agent_relevance: Suggests the agent should state which abstraction level its output belongs to and what else in the system it touches.

source: Chang Lee and Rondinelli (2026) Can Autonomous LLM Agents Execute Multireference Quantum Chemistry Calculations?
finding: Expert-derived decision ladder (a prioritised list of diagnose-and-fix rules) added to an LLM agent. Note: this is a rule list in the spirit of expert heuristics, not Rasmussen's decision ladder of information-processing stages.
numbers: 558 vertical transition energies from QUESTDB. Baseline agent 24.9% coverage, MAE 0.373 eV; with ladder 44.1% coverage, MAE 0.339 eV. Scored VTEs 139 to 246; R2 0.713 to 0.832. Doubles: baseline 0 verified, with ladder 14 of 30 (46.7%). Singles: 124 to 165 scored, MAE 0.384 to 0.332 eV.
limits: Single domain, single paper, preprint (Sep 2026). Name overlap with Rasmussen's term is a trap when searching. Ladder is described as heuristics that do not override the model.
agent_relevance: Written expert procedure, applied when a failure signal appears, lifts coverage a lot. Matches our rules to act on a real failure output.

source: Chang Lee and Rondinelli (2026) reproduction with full workflow information
finding: Given the complete published workflow, the agent reproduces calculations; the hard part is the workflow knowledge, not execution.
numbers: MAE 23 meV vs published QUEST values; 75% of target configurations resolved within seven attempts.
limits: Reproduction with the workflow in hand is an upper bound, not a fresh-problem result.
agent_relevance: The gap between 44% (procedure only) and 75% (full workflow) measures how much job knowledge the scaffold cannot yet supply.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap via Models of Decision-Making: Remediating Math Mistakes (Bridge)
finding: Cognitive task analysis (CTA) with experts yields a three-step decision model: (A) identify the error, (B) pick a remediation strategy, (C) pick an intention. Feeding expert decisions into the prompt greatly improves human-judged response quality.
numbers: 700 real tutoring conversations annotated by experts. GPT-4 with expert decisions is +76% more preferred and +80% more useful than GPT-4 with none; random decisions cut quality by 97% vs expert decisions. Gap between experts and models without the decision model: up to 2.6x overall. Improvement significant for all models (two-tailed t-test, p<0.05).
limits: Single task (math mistake remediation), grade 1-2 tutoring. Human raters, 3 per item. Expert decisions are oracle inputs; real use needs the model to choose them.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence that an expert decision model found by task analysis beats a plain prompt. Also shows wrong decisions are worse than none.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Bridge self decision-making condition
finding: Letting the model pick its own decisions helps strong models but not weak ones.
numbers: llama-2 and gpt-4 in the self decision condition beat no-decision on prefer and useful (p<0.05, up to +95%); gpt-3.5-turbo did not improve, because it chose correct-the-mistake almost every time (low path entropy; expert paths more diverse).
limits: Entropy comparison is descriptive.
agent_relevance: The model's own choice of problem class or strategy is only as good as its model; code or expert tables should do the gating (section 1: program decides, model fills slots).

source: Shao et al. (2025) Future of Work with AI Agents: Auditing Automation and Augmentation Potential across the U.S. Workforce
finding: Task-level work analysis at scale: WORKBank, built on O*NET tasks, pairs worker desires with AI-expert capability ratings and introduces a Human Agency Scale (H1-H5).
numbers: 1,500 domain workers, 844 tasks, 104 occupations. 46.1% of tasks: workers positive about automation; top reason free-up-time-for-high-value-work 69.38%; repetitive 46.6%. 28.0% of workers voiced fears. 26.9% of tasks have matching worker and expert agency levels; 45.2% of occupations have H3 (equal partnership) as dominant level.
limits: Self-report and expert opinion of capability, not measured performance. US only. Preprint v3 Feb 2026.
agent_relevance: Gives a goals-and-values layer for S0: before acting, ask which parts of the job the human wants to keep. A model for an owns-this-decision flag.

source: Shao et al. (2025) WORKBank investment mismatch
finding: Agent builders target the wrong tasks relative to worker desire and capability.
numbers: 41.0% of Y Combinator company-task mappings fall in the Low Priority or Automation Red Light zones; high-desire tasks are under-addressed. Occupations with the highest average automation desire make up only 1.26% of Claude usage.
limits: YC mapping done from company descriptions.
agent_relevance: Domain analysis predicts where agent effort is wasted. Weak direct link to a single-agent scaffold.

source: Shao et al. (2025) WORKBank human agency profiles
finding: Workers want more human involvement than AI experts judge necessary.
numbers: 47.5% of tasks fall in the triangle where workers prefer more human agency than experts rate as needed; occupation-level dominant levels H3 45.2%, H2 35.6%, H4 16.3%, H1 1.9%, H5 1.0%.
limits: Percentages read from figure text as printed.
agent_relevance: Support for human-in-loop handoff points as part of the S0 problem description.

source: Handa et al. (2025) Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations
finding: Maps over four million Claude.ai conversations onto O*NET tasks and occupations (a task-level work taxonomy used on LLM usage logs).
numbers: Software development and writing are nearly half of use; Computer and Mathematical occupations 37.2% of queries. 36% of occupations use AI for at least 25% of their tasks; about 4% for 75% or more; about 11% for half or more. 57% augmentation vs 43% automation.
limits: One platform; conversations mapped by a model-based classifier; shows use, not value or quality. Preprint, Feb 2025.
agent_relevance: Real use concentrates in tasks with clear, checkable structure; weight our problem classes the same way.

source: Handa et al. (2025) observed use vs exposure forecasts
finding: Observed use is lower than earlier task-exposure forecasts.
numbers: Eloundou et al. forecast about 80% of US workers have at least 10% of tasks affected; Handa observes about 57% of occupations using AI for at least 10% of tasks.
limits: Observed on one platform at one time; the forecast was about possible exposure, not use.
agent_relevance: Forecasts from task lists overstate what is done; the agent should not infer capability from a task title.

source: Xu et al. (2025) TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
finding: Benchmark of 175 tasks in a simulated software company, tasks drawn from the O*NET list plus expert introspection; agents browse, code and talk to simulated colleagues.
numbers: Best agent, Gemini 2.5 Pro with OpenHands, completes 30.3% of tasks and scores 39.3% with partial credit, about 27 steps and $4.2 per task. Claude 3.7 Sonnet 26.3%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 24.0%, GPT-4o 8.6%. Data science, admin and finance tasks lowest; software engineering highest.
quote: LLMs fail these seemingly easier tasks due to lack of ability to understand documents, communicate with other people
limits: Tasks are author-built, not a random sample of real jobs; authors caution against generalising to occupations. Simulated colleagues are Claude-backed.
agent_relevance: Job difficulty for agents does not follow human skill barriers. A work-domain map should score tasks by interaction type (social, UI, documents), not by prestige.

source: Xu et al. (2025) TheAgentCompany platform breakdown
finding: Agents fail most where the work involves colleagues and complex office UIs.
numbers: Most models struggle on RocketChat (social interaction) and ownCloud (online office suite). Llama 3.3 70B reaches 6.9%, on par with Llama 3.1 405B.
limits: Breakdown by required platform; tasks can use several platforms.
agent_relevance: Constraints of the work environment (who must be asked, which tool) are what the agent misses; this is the work-domain constraint layer.

source: Patwardhan et al. (2025) GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
finding: Benchmark built from O*NET and BLS work activities: 44 occupations, 9 sectors, tasks written by professionals with an average of 14 years of experience.
numbers: Gold subset 220 tasks. Claude Opus 4.1: 47.6% of deliverables graded better than or as good as the human expert's. Win rates: gpt-4o 12.5%, o4-mini 29.1%, o3 35.2%, gpt-5 39.0%. Each model sampled 3 times, graded by 3 human graders (9 comparisons per prompt). Automated grader agrees 66% with expert graders.
limits: Tasks are precisely specified one-shot deliverables; real work needs context discovery. Review time and cost of catastrophic mistakes not counted (authors' caveat).
agent_relevance: Shows how a work-activity taxonomy becomes an evaluation. Performance rises roughly linearly with model release date.

source: Patwardhan et al. (2025) GDPval scaffolding and prompt effects
finding: More reasoning effort, an explicit check-your-deliverable prompt, and best-of-4 with a judge each improve GPT-5 on work tasks.
numbers: Prompt raised human win rate by 5 percentage points; black-square artifacts, which affected over half of generated PDFs, were eliminated; egregious PowerPoint formatting errors fell from 86% to 64%; agents inspecting their deliverables rose from 15% to 97%. Best-of-N with N=4 and a GPT-5 judge was added to the scaffolding.
limits: Judge is the same family as the model (self-preference risk). Gains mix three changes.
agent_relevance: A general prompt that makes the agent check the artifact against the job's output requirements gives a cheap, measurable gain.

source: Motoura et al. (2018) Translating MFM into FOL: towards plant operation planning
finding: Older AI system on a means-ends functional model: multilevel flow modeling (MFM, from Lind, a relative of the abstraction hierarchy) translated to first-order logic so abductive reasoners can plan plant operation.
numbers: Demonstrated on one toy plant planning task solved by abduction; no benchmark numbers.
limits: Toy example only; 2018 short paper; no human or LLM comparison.
agent_relevance: A work-domain model can drive a formal planner. Possible bridge: model goals and functions as a graph, let code plan, model only fills text.

source: Di Matteo et al. (2024) An Abstraction Hierarchy Toward Productive Quantum Programming
finding: Software-stack abstraction hierarchy (three layers borrowed from parallel computing), not Rasmussen's functional hierarchy. Argues that a good hierarchy abstracts without hiding what matters.
numbers: No experiment; proposes layers and maps eigenvalue estimation onto them.
limits: Name overlap only. Do not count as evidence for Rasmussen-style work domain analysis.
agent_relevance: Warning for search: abstraction hierarchy in AI mostly means software or memory layers, not work-domain analysis.

source: Search note: arXiv listing queries run this session
finding: Direct arXiv queries found almost nothing that tests Rasmussen-style work domain analysis or the abstraction hierarchy on LLMs. work domain analysis: 0 results; cognitive work analysis: 1 (Figueiredo); multilevel flow modeling: 1 (2018); hierarchical task analysis plus LLM: 1 (ASHiTA); abstraction hierarchy plus language model: 6, none Rasmussen-style.
numbers: OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and the arXiv API were rate-limited and the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted, so journal literature (Ergonomics, Applied Ergonomics, Cognition Technology and Work) was not searched.
limits: Absence on arXiv is weak evidence: the CWA community publishes mostly in journals. Coverage is a lower bound.
agent_relevance: The gap is real: no controlled study found where an LLM agent was scaffolded with an abstraction hierarchy or Rasmussen decision ladder and compared to a plain agent. Our own test would be new.

source: Rasmussen (1986) Information Processing and Human-Machine Interaction; Vicente (1999) Cognitive Work Analysis (background, not opened)
finding: Founding sources for the abstraction hierarchy (functional purpose, abstract function, general function, physical function, physical form, linked by means-ends) and the decision ladder. Not read this session.
numbers: No figures recorded because not opened.
limits: Cited from memory only. Treat as pointers; earlier E13 documents may hold opened versions.
agent_relevance: Source of the levels our agent would use for S0 if we adopt the idea.
